title: Closest pair of points: brute force vs divide and conquer
problem_statement: Given n >= 2 points in the plane with integer coordinates (duplicates allowed), compute the minimum squared Euclidean distance (x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2 over all pairs i != j, as an exact integer.

input.size_measure: 2n integer coordinates (bounded by 10^9 in the harness, so arithmetic and comparisons are unit cost).

algorithms.name: all pairs
algorithms.idea: Compute the squared distance of every pair and keep the minimum.
algorithms.pseudocode: best = min over i < j of (x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) (exactly n(n-1)/2 distance evaluations on every input; PROOFS.md sections 1 and 3)

algorithms.name: Shamos-Hoey divide and conquer
algorithms.idea: Sort by x once; split at the median, solve both halves recursively, and let delta^2 be the better answer. A closer cross pair must lie in the vertical strip of half-width delta around the split; scanning the strip in y order, each point needs comparing only with the next few (at most 7). Each call returns its points sorted by y by merging its halves' lists, so no re-sorting is needed.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n log n) on every input, assuming the built-in sort runs in O(n log n) (machine-model assumption, listed under background; it covers the initial sort of the n points, the sort of at most 3 points in each leaf of the recursion, 1 + #leaves calls in all with at most n/2 leaves, for example 489 calls at n = 1000, and the min() calls: over at most 3 values in each leaf and over 2 values, min(best_l, best_r), in each of the #leaves - 1 internal calls, 2 #leaves - 1 calls in all, 975 at n = 1000). The work outside these built-in calls is Theta(n log n), proved in PROOFS.md section 5 (T(n) = T(floor(n/2)) + T(ceil(n/2)) + Theta(n): linear merge, strip filter, and at most 8 strip steps per strip point), and the lower bound Omega(n log n) holds on every input without the assumption
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n) under the same assumption: at most 5n + ceil(log2 n) + 6 words in the lists of the implementation's own code, plus the built-in sort's working space, which the assumption takes to be O(n) (PROOFS.md section 6)
algorithms.correctness: Shamos & Hoey 1975; Bentley & Shamos 1976. With xm the x of the right half's leftmost point, every left point has x <= xm and every right point x >= xm, so a cross pair at squared distance < delta^2 has both points within horizontal distance delta of xm. Strip points of one half are pairwise >= delta apart, so a delta x 2delta box holds at most 8 strip points: the inner scan stops after O(1) steps, and it stops early only once dy^2 >= the current best. Complete proof: PROOFS.md sections 4-5.

shape.note: count depends on the drawn instance; kept so the record says why the diagnostic cannot decide

relationship: Both polynomial: Theta(n^2) -> Theta(n log n), the divide-and-conquer bound assuming the built-in sort runs in O(n log n) (background), so the T3 tag rests on that assumption (PROOFS.md sections 3, 5 and 7). The minimum distance is 0 exactly when two points coincide, so element distinctness reduces to closest pair (take the points (x_i, 0); PROOFS.md section 7). Conditional optimality: if the background lower bound for element distinctness in the algebraic computation tree model on real-valued inputs holds (Ben-Or 1983), the reduction gives Omega(n log n) for closest pair in that model, and divide and conquer matches it up to a constant factor under the sort assumption. That lower bound is about real-valued inputs; it does not by itself give a lower bound for the integer coordinates used here, and it does not cover algorithms that use the floor function. Randomized closest-pair algorithms are listed under background.

sources.note: Background only. The file dates from 2002 (T. Peters); the cited passage, which states that the code uses the powersort merge strategy of Munro and Wild, is a later addition. Read in the current version of the main branch on 2026-10-07.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree for n = 2..9, 16, 17, 33, 100 and 500 (all pairs capped at n = 500; divide and conquer also at n = 3000) on three instance kinds: generic coordinates in [0, 10^6), a tiny grid of side ~sqrt(n) (duplicate points, answer 0, collinear points), and all points on one vertical line (every point lands in the strip). harness.check is an exact, independent oracle: a plane sweep with pruning along the coordinate of larger spread. V2 (since 2026-10-07, research/2026-10-07b_count_based_v2.md): on points with coordinates in [0, 10^9), the measured quantity is the exact number of MULTIPLICATIONS (a squaring ** 2 counts as one) made by the unchanged implementations, counted by an instrumented integer type (CountingInt in harness.py) that wraps every coordinate; with it both implementations return the same answers as on plain integers (checked at n = 2, 3, 4, 7, 50, 300). All pairs: exactly n(n-1) at n = 125, 250, 500, 1000, 2000 (15500 ... 3998000); alpha = 1.001 against n^2. Divide and conquer, 1 seeded instance per n: 14523, 31335, 68047, 147196, 314573, 674959, 1436363 at n = 1000, 2000, ..., 64000 (1.406 to 1.457 n log2 n), of which the strip filter contributes S(n) = n + S(floor(n/2)) + S(ceil(n/2)) (exactly, e.g. 955392 at n = 64000), the base cases 2 per pair, and the data-dependent strip scan the rest (29% to 31%); alpha = 0.993 against n log n (0.993 to 0.995 over three seeded samples). Comparisons are not counted: those made inside CPython's sorted() and min() differ between Python versions (39380 under Python 3.12.10 vs 39445 under 3.14.2 at n = 1000, experiments/2026-10-07b_count_v2_cross_version.py), whereas the reported multiplication counts are identical under both. Tolerance 0.03: exact counts carry no timing noise, so the band only covers lower-order terms and the data-dependent strip scan (largest |alpha - 1| here 0.007) and stays below half the distance to the nearest rival. Rivals that must NOT fit, all rejected: all pairs against n log n (alpha = 1.721) and n^2 log n (0.926); divide and conquer against n (1.105), n log^2 n (0.902) and n^2 (0.553). The log factor is therefore resolved for both (validator diagnostic, RESEARCH_LOG RL-048). experiments/2026-10-07b_count_v2_closest_pair.py reproduces every count above. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry from the code (the exact counts on their domains, correctness of both algorithms, the packing lemma, the time and space bounds, and the reduction from element distinctness) and names the deterministic checks of each, among them tests/test_proofs_closest_pair.py; the upper time and space bounds of divide and conquer hold under the machine-model assumption on the built-in sort (background).

caveats: Squared distances on integer coordinates keep every value exact (Python integers), and the proofs in PROOFS.md use this exactness; floating-point coordinates are outside the problem statement. V2 counts multiplications, not time: 61.5% to 66.5% (measured) of the divide-and-conquer count (n = 1000..64000) is the strip filter's one squaring per point per recursion level (n per level over about log2 n levels); the comparisons of the built-in sorts and of the merges are not counted. The earlier timing fit could not distinguish n log n from n over the measured range (the log factor varies by only ~1.6x); the exact counts do. The Omega(n log n) lower bound is background (Ben-Or 1983): it holds for algebraic computation trees on real-valued inputs, it is not a theorem about this entry's integer inputs, and it does not cover algorithms that use the floor function.
notes: Related literature and the machine-model assumption on the built-in sort are listed under background.

background.statement: Any algebraic computation tree that decides element distinctness (are n real numbers pairwise distinct?) has worst-case complexity Omega(n log n); the general bound is in terms of the number of connected components of the set of yes-inputs.
Randomized closest-pair algorithms: Rabin 1976; Khuller & Matias 1995 ('A simple randomized sieve algorithm for the closest-pair problem'). Their models and bounds are not restated here.
Divide-and-conquer algorithms in multidimensional space: Bentley & Shamos 1976. Their bounds are not restated here.

Machine-model assumption of this entry: the built-in sort (sorted() and list.sort()) runs in O(n log n) comparisons and time, with O(n) extra space, in the worst case on n items (so in O(1) time on at most 3 items), and min() over k values takes O(k) time. Basis, as far as the sources go: the current CPython list sort orders its merges by the powersort rule of Munro and Wild (listsort.txt), and with a plain merge powersort makes at most n H + 3n - r <= n log2 n + 3n comparisons on n items forming r runs, where H is the entropy of the run lengths (Munro & Wild 2018, Theorem 6 of the arXiv version). CPython's merges also gallop, which that theorem does not cover, so the assumption is not proved in this repository.
background.source: Munro & Wild 2018, Theorem 6 (arXiv version), for the plain-merge bound; Python Software Foundation, Objects/listsort.txt, for the merge order of the current CPython list sort
